newsitem.title: USA: U.S. TOBACCO CO ADMITS SMOKING IS HEALTH HAZARD.
newsitem.headline: U.S. TOBACCO CO ADMITS SMOKING IS HEALTH HAZARD.

text.p: In the harshest blow yet to the cigarette industry, Liggett Group agreed Thursday to settle tobacco litigation with almost half of the nation's attorneys general and give up potentially devastating documents.
The historic accord calls for unprecedented concessions from Liggett, owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Ltd.
The tobacco company agreed to allow current and former employees -- including its lawyers -- to testify against the rest of the industry.
The accord was reached with all 22 state attorneys general who have sued the industry to recoup Medicaid health care costs of treating smokers.
Liggett became the first tobacco company to admit the health hazards of smoking and the addictiveness. It has agreed to include labels on its cigarettes warning about the hazards of nicotine.

"I believe this is the beginning of the end for this conspiracy of lies and deception that has been perpetrated on the American public by the tobacco companies. Somebody is finally telling the truth," Arizona Attorney General Grant Woods told a news conference.

Liggett, the smallest of the major U.S. cigarette makers, admitted companies actively targeted teenagers. "Liggett says publicly and for first time that for any tobacco executive, for any tobacco company, for any person to say contrary, is a lie. They know it and they will help us prove it," Woods said.

The other tobacco companies denied that they market cigarettes to minors and in a joint statement dismissed the deal as a "desperate attempt" by LeBow to get another cigarette manufacturer to take over his "financially troubled and failing tobacco interests."
"The only ones who potentially benefit from LeBow's latest shenanigans are plaintiffs' lawyers," they said.
Regardless of Bennett's motives, the settlement could prove damaging to other tobacco companies on many fronts.

Among the most devastating effects is that the documents might be used by the Justice Department, which is investigating the industry for criminal wrongdoing and probing whether top executives lied to Congress when they testified in 1994 that nicotine is not addictive.
The attorneys general said they might also use the documents to bring criminal cases in their individual states.

Mississippi Attorney Michael Moore, who has spearheaded the litigation, said the agreement by Liggett to turn over evidence and allow employees and counsel to testify will bring the industry "to its knees."
"Never again will Big Tobacco be able to claim innocence with a straight face," he said. The Mississippi case is to be the first Medicaid case to go to trial on June 2.
The Liggett accord includes a settlement in which Liggett will pay states 25 percent of its pretax profits for the next 25 years to settle claims.

Tobacco stocks tumbled as word of the settlement spread. Philip Morris Cos. Inc., the world's largest cigarette maker, fell $6.125 to $115.875, Loews Corp., which owns Lorillard tobacco, lost $2.25 to $98.50 and American Brands fell $1.125 to $50.25, all on the New York Stock Exchange. Brooke Group rose 62.5 cents to $4.875.
